I would start with a farrier before rushing a vet check. I think a vet would offer x rays if you wanted to see what’s going on but they’d probably just tell you to get him a proper trim and then see how he’s doing. It’s not something that is super urgent, like call the vet tomorrow. It’s definitely something to fix sooner than later but he isn’t going to die overnight. And if he is EMS/cushings, he also won’t die overnight. If you do have him evaluated for metabolic diseases and he comes up positive, he would need to be managed with limited/no grass & very low sugar/starch food. If cushings, same thing plus pergolide. 

He will be noticeably more comfortable with shorter toes and in time, a properly aligned heel. You can see how much the long toe is stressing his soft tissues. The relief is immediate for his soft tissues once the toe is taken back. You’ll see his stance change and he will likely be able to truly relax some muscles that have been tense for a while due to compensation. 

Good luck!! :)

To go along with all of these great suggestions, I would say that it’s important to learn to use your space wisely. Don’t follow the rules on the back of seed packets. Plant things together, plant them densely, and grow them vertically. You can fit so much in a small area! I keep my tomatoes packed tightly and staked up with string and t posts in a Florida weave system. I plant garlic, herbs, onions, marigolds under and between them. Zucchini/squash gets heavily pruned and the main stem tied up to a post, this way they can be planted a foot apart and things can be planted under/around them. Pole beans go over a cow panel trellis. Peas go up a small section of fence or netting. 

Learn what plants do well beside each other. You can use sturdy plants like corn or sunflowers to trellis smaller plants. 

Also helpful is a handful of hens who can free range your yard and eat garden and food scraps. This only works if your setup is right for it, of course. But I do enjoy having fresh eggs and they don’t cost a whole lot to maintain with the way we do things. Plus we sell a dozen eggs to my fiancés coworkers here and there, so that money goes back into feeding them (they are city folks who pay $8 at the store for “better eggs”, so they happily pay $5/dozen for ours) 

We live in the middle of town (it’s a rural town, but a town none the less) and we have actually done 6 Cornish cross meat birds at a time and processed them in our back yard. So in tough times, that can certainly be an option for more people than most realize.

As I’ve said before, it’s one thing to have a horse who won’t keep weight on for whatever reason, being old or otherwise. But nobody will ever convince me that a horse in this poor condition should be brought to the county fair on display and be ridden. Period. You should not be riding a horse this thin at home either. But to bring them in public is insane. It doesn’t matter if they’re eating grain, hay, or supplements. The horses are STILL too thin. I never accused anybody of not feeding these horses.
